paper_title: Towards Predicting Any Human Trajectory In Context
caption: Performance of random example selection and the proposed STES at varying numbers of in-context examples with a larger number of examples
model_annotation: The line chart displays the performance of two methods—“ST-ES” and “Random”—in terms of minADE₂₀ (a trajectory prediction error metric) as a function of the number of in-context examples, ranging from 0 to 15. The x-axis, labeled “Number of Examples,” is linearly scaled with tick marks at integer intervals from 0 to 15. The y-axis, labeled “minADE₂₀ (↑),” is linearly scaled from approximately 14.8 to 17.1, with major grid lines and tick labels at 0.5-unit intervals (15.0, 15.5, 16.0, 16.5, 17.0). The blue line with circular markers, labeled “ST-ES,” begins at approximately 17.05 when the number of examples is 0, drops sharply to 15.15 at 1 example, then gradually declines to a minimum of approximately 14.85 around 10 examples before slightly rising to 14.9 at 15 examples. The orange line with circular markers, labeled “Random,” starts at approximately 16.8 at 0 examples, decreases slightly to 16.5 by 1 example, then remains relatively flat, fluctuating between 16.45 and 16.5 across examples 2 through 15. Both lines are solid and use circular markers at each data point.

model_annotations.English: The line plot illustrates the performance of two methods—ST-ES (blue line with circular markers) and Random (orange line with circular markers)—in terms of minADE₂₀ (lower is better) as the number of in-context examples increases from 0 to 15. The x-axis, labeled “Number of Examples,” is linearly scaled from 0 to 15 with tick marks at integer intervals. The y-axis, labeled “minADE₂₀ (↓),” is linearly scaled from approximately 14.8 to 17.1, with major grid lines at 0.5 intervals. The ST-ES method starts at minADE₂₀ ≈ 17.05 at 0 examples, drops sharply to ≈15.1 at 1 example, then gradually decreases to a minimum near 14.85 around 10–12 examples before slightly rising to ≈14.9 at 15 examples. The Random method begins at ≈16.8 at 0 examples, drops slightly to ≈16.5 at 1 example, then remains relatively stable between 16.45 and 16.5 across the remaining examples, showing minimal improvement with more examples. Both lines are solid and marked with circular data points at each integer x-value.
